---
title: "Logistic and Discriminant Methods"
---

Classification models estimate class membership. This chapter focuses
on probability-based classifiers: logistic regression, linear
discriminant analysis, and quadratic discriminant analysis.

## Learning Objectives

- Explain why ordinary linear regression is not appropriate for binary
  outcomes.
- Fit and interpret logistic regression.
- Interpret log odds, odds ratios, fitted probabilities, and thresholds.
- Compare logistic regression with LDA and QDA.
- Evaluate classifiers with confusion matrices, sensitivity,
  specificity, ROC curves, AUC, and calibration.

## Logistic Regression

For a binary outcome, logistic regression models

$$
p(x) = \Pr(Y = 1 \mid X=x).
$$

The logit link maps probabilities to the real line:

$$
\log\left(\frac{p(x)}{1-p(x)}\right)
= \beta_0 + x^\top\beta.
$$

Equivalently,

$$
p(x) =
\frac{\exp(\beta_0 + x^\top\beta)}
{1 + \exp(\beta_0 + x^\top\beta)}.
$$

Coefficients are changes in log odds. Exponentiating a coefficient
gives an odds ratio, holding the other predictors fixed.

## Credit Default Example

The default data show why probability estimation matters. The response
is rare, so accuracy can be misleading: a classifier that predicts "no
default" for everyone may have high accuracy but no practical value.

```r
library(ISLR)

default_fit <- glm(
  default ~ student + balance + income,
  data = Default,
  family = binomial
)

summary(default_fit)
exp(coef(default_fit))
Default$prob_default <- predict(default_fit, type = "response")
```

The fitted probabilities can be sorted, binned, and compared with
observed default rates. This helps students see whether high predicted
risk actually corresponds to higher observed risk.

## Thresholds and Error Costs

Logistic regression returns probabilities. A threshold turns
probabilities into class labels:

```r
pred_class <- ifelse(Default$prob_default > 0.5, "Yes", "No")
table(predicted = pred_class, observed = Default$default)
```

The threshold should reflect the decision context. If false negatives
are expensive, a lower threshold may be appropriate. If false positives
are expensive, a higher threshold may be appropriate. The statistical
model estimates risk; the threshold encodes a decision rule.

## Discriminant Analysis

Discriminant analysis starts by modeling the distribution of predictors
within each class. Bayes' rule gives

$$
\Pr(Y=k \mid X=x)
=
\frac{\pi_k f_k(x)}
{\sum_{\ell=1}^{K} \pi_\ell f_\ell(x)},
$$

where $\pi_k$ is the prior probability of class $k$ and $f_k(x)$ is the
class-conditional density.

LDA assumes that each class has a multivariate normal predictor
distribution with a common covariance matrix. This produces linear
decision boundaries. QDA allows a different covariance matrix in each
class, producing quadratic boundaries.

```r
library(MASS)

lda_fit <- lda(default ~ balance + income + student, data = Default)
qda_fit <- qda(default ~ balance + income + student, data = Default)

lda_pred <- predict(lda_fit)$posterior[, "Yes"]
qda_pred <- predict(qda_fit)$posterior[, "Yes"]
```

LDA can be more stable when data are limited because it estimates fewer
parameters. QDA can be more flexible when class covariance patterns
really differ and there is enough data to estimate them.

## ROC, AUC, and Calibration

Classification evaluation should include more than one number:

| Measure | What it answers |
|---|---|
| Accuracy | What fraction of labels are correct at one threshold? |
| Sensitivity | What fraction of positives are detected? |
| Specificity | What fraction of negatives are correctly rejected? |
| ROC curve | How do sensitivity and specificity trade off across thresholds? |
| AUC | How well are positives ranked above negatives? |
| Calibration | Do predicted probabilities match observed frequencies? |

ROC curves evaluate ranking across thresholds. Calibration evaluates
probability quality. A model can rank well and still produce poorly
calibrated probabilities.

## Chapter Synthesis

Fit logistic regression, LDA, and QDA to the same binary classification
problem. Compare fitted probabilities, confusion matrices at multiple
thresholds, ROC curves, AUC, and calibration. State which model is best
for probability estimation and which threshold is appropriate for the
decision context.
